short_title: Re: Dropping from the Rolls of Miras
full_title: RE: DROPPING FROM THE ROLLS OF MS. MAILYN E. MIRAS, STENOGRAPHER III, BRANCH 65, REGIONAL TRIAL COURT, INFANTA, QUEZON.
subject: Political and Public International Law
syllabus_topic: XI. Law on Public Officers > B. Public Office > 9. Termination of Official Relation
topics: Dropping from the rolls for AWOL of at least 30 working days (2025 RACCS, Rule 20, Section 132)
No prior notice required; notice of separation and 15-day appeal
Dropping from the rolls is non-disciplinary
Mere filing of a leave application does not authorize absence
doctrine:
Under **Rule 20, Section 132(A-1) of the 2025 Rules on Administrative Cases in the Civil Service (RACCS)** (CSC Resolution No. 2500357), **an official or employee who is continuously absent without official leave (AWOL) for at least 30 working days may be immediately dropped from the rolls without prior notice.** A notice of separation is issued at the employee's last known address, and the employee may appeal within 15 days from receipt. Failure to provide the notice does not invalidate the dropping, but the appeal period then runs from actual receipt of the notice.

**Dropping from the rolls is non-disciplinary** (2025 RACCS, Rule 20, Section 135): it does not forfeit any benefit or disqualify the employee from reemployment in the government. Its purpose is to address the disruption caused by continuous and prolonged AWOL by declaring the post vacant so it can be filled. Hence, the dismissal of criminal cases against the employee is irrelevant.

**Approval of a vacation leave is not presumed**; it depends on the needs of the service and the discretion of the head of office, so the mere filing of a leave application does not authorize an employee to be absent. Medical or psychological problems, or a feeling of being bullied by a supervisor, do not excuse an employee who stops reporting without waiting for the leave to be approved. The Court applied these settled rules and denied the appeal with finality.
facts:
Mailyn E. Miras was Court Stenographer III of RTC Branch 65, Infanta, Quezon. On July 22, 2020, she applied for sick leave, and on July 24, 2020, for 30 days of vacation leave. The Clerk of Court, Atty. Edward Justine R. Orden, recommended disapproval of both, and neither was acted upon by the presiding judge, who had been appointed to another court. Without waiting for action, Miras stopped reporting on July 27, 2020 and ignored a Return to Work Order sent on July 30, 2020. She came back only on September 23, 2020, after 43 working days, to accomplish her DTRs for July to December 2020. Atty. Orden refused to accept them and, on September 28, 2020, asked the OCA to drop her from the rolls.

OCA records showed that she had not submitted DTRs from July 2020 onward and had no approved leave for the period. The OCA also noted three pending administrative cases and numerous criminal cases for falsification of public documents, use of falsified documents and perjury against her. It recommended that she be dropped from the rolls for being AWOL for at least 30 days, without prejudice to those cases, and that her position be declared vacant under Rule 20, Section 107(a)(1) of the 2017 RACCS.

On October 9, 2023, the Court's First Division dropped Miras from the rolls effective July 1, 2020, retained the benefits she may be entitled to and her eligibility for reemployment in the government, declared her position vacant, and directed that she be notified. On March 27, 2024, she filed an untitled pleading seeking reconsideration, which the Court treated as an appeal. She claimed that Atty. Orden harassed her and kept recommending disapproval of her leaves although she was bleeding from a uterine myoma; that the criminal and administrative cases he filed, all the criminal cases having been dismissed, caused her an anxiety disorder that led to her long absence; and that being dropped without notice violated her right to due process.
issues: Whether Ms. Miras was validly dropped from the rolls, without prior notice, for being absent without approved leave.
Whether the dismissal of the criminal cases against her, her medical and psychological condition, or her supervisor's alleged harassment justify setting aside her dropping from the rolls.
ruling:
**1. Yes. Her dropping from the rolls was proper, and no prior notice was required.** Her conduct falls under Rule 20, Section 132(A-1) of the 2025 RACCS, under which an employee continuously AWOL for at least 30 working days "may be immediately dropped from the rolls without prior notice," subject to a notice of separation at the last known address and the right to appeal within 15 days from receipt; failure to provide the notice does not invalidate the dropping. The Court read the provision as clear that "no prior notice is required" to drop such an employee. Her AWOL was proved by the OAS-OCA records of her failure to submit DTRs and bundy cards, the absence of any approved leave for the period, and the undisputed fact that she ignored a written order to return to work.

**2. No.** **Dropping from the rolls is non-disciplinary** under Rule 20, Section 135 of the 2025 RACCS; it does not forfeit benefits or disqualify from reemployment. It addresses the disruption caused by continuous and prolonged AWOL by removing employees who have effectively abandoned their posts, "without the stigma or penalties attendant to disciplinary dismissal." **The dismissal of the criminal cases was therefore irrelevant** to her 43 working days of absence without approved leave. She was also wrong to stop reporting because of her medical and psychological problems or because she felt bullied; she should have waited for the approval of her vacation leave. **"The approval of a vacation leave is not automatically presumed"**; it depends on the needs of the service and the discretion of the head of the agency, and "[t]he mere filing of a vacation leave application does not authorize an employee to be absent." Her refusal to return when ordered, and her 43-working-day absence although she applied for only 30 days of leave, showed a "recalcitrant attitude and willful intention to be absent." Her AWOL prejudiced the public service: public office is a public trust, and those in the administration of justice must uphold public accountability.
disposition: Ms. Miras's appeal from the October 9, 2023 Resolution, which dropped her from the rolls effective July 1, 2020, declared her position of Court Stenographer III, RTC Branch 65, Infanta, Quezon vacant, and informed her of her separation from the service, was DENIED with finality.

bar_questions.q: Liza, a Clerk III in a municipal trial court, stopped reporting for work and did not file any leave application. After she had been continuously absent for 35 working days, the Supreme Court, on the OCA's recommendation, dropped her from the rolls without first notifying her or asking her to explain. No notice of separation was sent to her last known address; she learned of it only when a co-employee handed her a copy months later. (a) Was Liza denied due process? (b) Did the failure to send her the notice of separation invalidate her dropping from the rolls, and from when may she appeal?

alac.answer: (a) No. An employee continuously AWOL for at least 30 working days may be dropped from the rolls without prior notice. (b) No. The failure to send the notice of separation does not invalidate the dropping, but her 15-day period to appeal runs from her actual receipt of the notice.
alac.legal_basis: Under Rule 20, Section 132(A-1) of the 2025 RACCS, an official or employee continuously on AWOL for at least 30 working days may be immediately dropped from the rolls without prior notice. A notice of separation is issued at the last known address, and the employee may appeal within 15 days from receipt. Failure to provide a notice of separation does not invalidate the dropping, but the right to appeal is counted from the employee's actual receipt of the notice. In Re: Dropping from the Rolls of Miras (A.M. No. 23-08-55-RTC, November 5, 2025), the Court applied this provision and held that no prior notice is required to drop an employee continuously AWOL for at least 30 working days.
alac.application: Liza was continuously absent for 35 working days without any leave application, beyond the 30-working-day threshold. The rule allows her to be dropped immediately without prior notice, so the lack of a prior chance to explain does not violate due process; her remedy is to appeal once she is notified of her separation. Since no notice of separation was sent to her, the dropping remains valid, but her 15 days to appeal began only when she actually received the notice from her co-employee.
alac.conclusion: Liza was validly dropped from the rolls without prior notice, and she may appeal within 15 days from her actual receipt of the notice of separation.

bar_questions.q: Rico, a court interpreter, filed an application for 30 days of vacation leave. His branch clerk of court recommended disapproval, and the presiding judge never acted on it. Rico stopped reporting the next day, ignored a written order to return to work, and came back after 45 working days. He argues that his leave should be deemed approved because it was never acted upon, and that he was suffering from anxiety caused by his supervisor's harassment. May Rico be dropped from the rolls?

alac.answer: Yes. Rico was continuously absent without approved leave for more than 30 working days and may be dropped from the rolls.
alac.legal_basis: Under Rule 20, Section 132(A-1) of the 2025 RACCS, an employee continuously on AWOL for at least 30 working days may be dropped from the rolls without prior notice. In Re: Dropping from the Rolls of Miras (A.M. No. 23-08-55-RTC, November 5, 2025), the Court held that the approval of a vacation leave is not automatically presumed but depends on the needs of the service and the discretion of the head of office, so the mere filing of a leave application does not authorize an employee to be absent. It also held that medical or psychological problems, or a feeling of being bullied by a supervisor, did not justify absenting oneself without waiting for the leave to be approved, especially where the employee ignored an order to return to work.
alac.application: Rico's leave application was never approved, and its mere filing did not authorize him to stop reporting. He also ignored a written order to return and stayed away for 45 working days, longer than the 30 days he applied for, which shows a willful intention to be absent. His anxiety and his complaints against his supervisor did not excuse him from waiting for action on his leave.
alac.conclusion: Rico may be dropped from the rolls for being continuously absent without approved leave for more than 30 working days.

bar_questions.q: Nora, a court stenographer, was dropped from the rolls for being absent without approved leave for 40 working days. On appeal, she argues that (a) being dropped from the rolls will forfeit her accrued benefits and bar her from any future government employment, and (b) she should be reinstated because the falsification cases her supervisor filed against her were all dismissed. Rule on her arguments.

alac.answer: (a) Nora is mistaken; dropping from the rolls does not forfeit her benefits or disqualify her from reemployment in the government. (b) The dismissal of the criminal cases does not warrant her reinstatement because it is irrelevant to her absence without leave.
alac.legal_basis: Under Rule 20, Section 135 of the 2025 RACCS, dropping from the rolls is non-disciplinary in nature and does not result in the forfeiture of any benefit or in disqualification from reemployment in the government. In Re: Dropping from the Rolls of Miras (A.M. No. 23-08-55-RTC, November 5, 2025), the Court explained that its purpose is to address the disruption caused by an employee's continuous and prolonged AWOL by declaring the position vacant so it can be filled, "without the stigma or penalties attendant to disciplinary dismissal"; hence, the dismissal of criminal cases against the employee was irrelevant to her continuous absence without approved leave.
alac.application: Nora's separation is not a penalty but a measure to fill a post she effectively abandoned, so she keeps the benefits she is entitled to under existing laws and may be reemployed in the government. The ground for her separation is her 40 working days of absence without approved leave, not the falsification charges, so their dismissal does not affect the validity of her dropping from the rolls.
alac.conclusion: Nora keeps her benefits and eligibility for reemployment, but her dropping from the rolls stands despite the dismissal of the criminal cases.

notes: The Court applied the 2025 RACCS (CSC Resolution No. 2500357), although the OCA had recommended dropping under Rule 20, Section 107(a)(1) of the 2017 RACCS. The E-Library text cites "Section 132(A-l)", read here as 132(A-1). The quoted Section 132 also says dropping must be done within 30 days from the time the ground arises, failing which the head of agency is barred; the Resolution did not discuss this point. As printed, the fallo numbers its items (1), (2) and (4), and it does not repeat the retention of benefits stated in the October 9, 2023 Resolution. The dropping took effect July 1, 2020, although the text says she stopped reporting on July 27, 2020; both dates are as printed.
